breaking.headline: Anthropic’s first trade still pending as indications point near $100
breaking.fact: Anthropic’s shares began trading on the Nasdaq today under the ticker ANT after pricing at $83 a share, but the first trade had still not printed by late morning as the opening auction ran — indications pointed to roughly $100–$107, about 20–24% above the IPO price, with the first trade expected around noon to 1 p.m. ET. The $81.3 billion offering is the largest IPO on record.

breaking.headline: Stocks reverse: Nasdaq gives up a 2% opening pop
breaking.fact: The Nasdaq 100 opened up nearly 2% on Anthropic’s debut but reversed to trade down on the day by mid-session, while the S&P 500 turned negative and the Dow fell about 1% — a fourth straight 1%+ Dow drop to start the week would have happened only twice since 1952. Fed Vice Chair Philip Jefferson said Thursday the AI buildout is adding to inflation.

breaking.headline: Philly Fed factory gauge plunges to 6.3, a six-month low
breaking.fact: Manufacturing activity in the Philadelphia region fell sharply in November: the Philly Fed’s current-activity index dropped to 6.3 from 20.9 in October, far below the roughly 20 economists expected, with new orders slipping into contraction at -0.4. Prices paid jumped to 58.2, its highest since April — weaker activity with higher prices, a tough mix for the Fed.

breaking.headline: Housing starts jump, but permits hit a 6½-year low
breaking.fact: U.S. housing starts jumped 9.9% in October to 1.309 million, beating expectations of 1.250 million, but building permits — a proxy for future construction — slumped 7.4% to 1.295 million, a 6½-year low and well below the 1.380 million expected. Pending home sales had already fallen to a record low in October.

weekInBrief.headline: Leading indicators fall 0.3% in October
weekInBrief.body: The Conference Board’s Leading Economic Index fell 0.3% to 99.3 in October, a fresh sign of cooling momentum alongside Thursday’s weak Philly Fed survey and jobless claims of 203,000 — above the 197,000 economists expected.

weekInBrief.headline: December hike now seen as near-certain, with a small chance of 50bp
weekInBrief.body: Minutes from the Fed’s October meeting showed nearly all participants favored a rate hike in December, and a couple said a move of more than 25 basis points could warrant consideration. Rate futures now price roughly a 95% chance of a quarter-point hike and about 5% for a half-point move, after Governor Christopher Waller said Wednesday the Fed may need 50bp to remind markets that 3% is not the inflation target.

weekInBrief.headline: Shoppers show up, homebuyers hold back
weekInBrief.body: Target said comparable transactions rose 5% from a year earlier — shoppers came more often, with a much smaller increase in spending per trip — while housing stays weak: October permits fell 7.4% to a 6½-year low and signed contracts for existing homes fell 4.7% to a record low.

weekInBrief.headline: Yen slides toward 160 per dollar as the dollar holds its high
weekInBrief.body: The dollar held near its 19-month high around 103.9 while the yen slid toward the key 160-per-dollar level, trading in the upper 159s in London, as resilient U.S. inflation data and hawkish Fed comments keep the dollar bid and traders price a near-certain December hike.

items.headline: Latest from the Strait
items.body: Iran’s military claimed on Wednesday that three commercial oil tankers caught fire and stopped dead in the water after striking naval mines east of the Strait of Hormuz — an Iranian state-media claim, uncorroborated so far. U.S. Central Command’s Wednesday advisory added a new enforcement detail: a ship that takes Iranian cargo in a ship-to-ship transfer may be ordered to proceed to the Iranian port where the cargo originated, and refusal to comply with boarding could bring enforcement action. On oil, Iranian crude exports have remained near a standstill for months, shipping sources told Reuters — but Tehran has still managed to export liquefied petroleum gas and jet fuel since July through the very ship-to-ship transfers Wednesday’s advisory now targets — while CENTCOM says U.S.-escorted non-Iranian crude keeps flowing through the strait.

space.headline: NASA reshapes Artemis: Starship to dock with Orion in Earth orbit first
space.body: NASA has restructured its Artemis lunar-landing approach: Starship will first dock with the Orion crew vehicle while both are still in Earth orbit, and only then will the combined stack travel to the Moon. The change eases trajectory constraints on the landers — SpaceX’s Starship and Blue Origin’s Blue Moon — but shifts extra responsibilities onto Orion, built by Lockheed Martin. NASA is targeting as soon as 2028 for Artemis IV, the first crewed Moon landing since Apollo.

space.headline: ULA points to fuel starvation in the Vulcan failure that cost Amazon 40 satellites
space.body: United Launch Alliance said Wednesday that preliminary findings point to an inadequate fuel supply to the BE-4 engines — not the engines themselves — as the cause of low thrust that doomed Sunday’s Vulcan launch, its first total mission failure since the joint venture formed in 2006. The rocket failed about 10 minutes into flight, losing 40 Amazon Leo internet satellites; the FAA will oversee the investigation and the rocket is grounded until fixes are approved. Amazon’s next Leo launch is an Ariane 6 mission targeted for Nov. 23 at the earliest.

space.headline: New spin effect switches antiferromagnets at room temperature
space.body: Northwestern researchers have discovered an effect they call octupole-driven spin-transfer torque, letting an electric current flip the magnetic state of noncollinear antiferromagnets at room temperature — a class of materials prized for fast, dense memory because they barely interact with outside magnetic fields. The team demonstrated it in nanoscale all-antiferromagnetic tunnel junctions; the work is published in Nature.

space.headline: Homo erectus survived in China’s rainforests far later than thought
space.body: Homo erectus was still surviving in southern China between 324,000 and 184,000 years ago — much later than previously accepted — and had adapted to dense tropical rainforest, an environment long thought to be the domain of only Homo sapiens. Teeth and thousands of fossils from two sister caves in Guangxi, dated with five independent techniques, show the species ranged farther and lived later than the textbooks said; the findings appear in two papers in Nature.
